Identification as Schleicher's fable is by content (sheep/wool/horses, same structure and many identical forms as his 2010 'Schleicher's fable' paper). No translation or notation notes given. Lines split at the four paragraph-initial indents / sentence-final periods; wrapped lines joined with single spaces. versions.english: A sheep that had no wool saw horses, one pulling a heavy cart, one carrying a big load, and one quickly carrying a man. The sheep said to the horses: My heart pains me seeing a man driving horses. The horses said: Listen sheep, our hearts pain us when we see that a man, the master, makes the wool of sheep into a warm garment for himself, and the sheep have no wool. Having heard this, the sheep fled into the plain.
versions.evidence_quote: Frederik Kortlandt, Leiden University, www.kortlandt.nl SCHLEICHER’S FABLE [...] As my chief concern has always been the relative chronology of linguistic developments, it may be appropriate to present my version of Schleicher’s fable for a number of successive reconstructed systems,
versions.notation_notes: Since the distinction between the three laryngeals was preserved in Greek (Central IE) and Armenian (satəm IE), it was not lost before Balto-Slavic times, when they merged with the glottalic feature of the PIE “unaspirated voiced” stops into a glottal stop (Winter’s law, cf. K263 = 2009: 44f.). [...] The word-final fortis stop became glottalic in the non-Anatolian languages (cf. K272 = 2010: 40).
versions.notes: Stage column headed 'PROTO-INDO-EUROPEAN' in the paper, which gives the fable for successive reconstructed systems (PIE, non-Anatolian IE, Classic IE, Central IE, satəm IE, Balto-Slavic, East Baltic, Lithuanian); the Balto-Slavic, East Baltic and Lithuanian columns are not PIE-lineage and were omitted. English is Kortlandt's 'Translation of the text (cf. Lehmann & Zgusta 1979: 456, 462)', given once for all stages; per-line English assigned by its four sentences. Lines split at sentence-final periods (4 sentences); table line breaks joined with single spaces. Paper has no notation section; notation_notes are verbatim commentary sentences from p.1. lines.source_form: to’d k̑ek̑luuṣ ʕʷeuiṣ pleʕnom ʔe bēu’g.
lines.english: Having heard this, the sheep fled into the plain.

versions.english: A sheep that had no wool saw horses, one pulling a heavy cart, one carrying a big load, and one quickly carrying a man. The sheep said to the horses: My heart pains me seeing a man driving horses. The horses said: Listen sheep, our hearts pain us when we see that a man, the master, makes the wool of sheep into a warm garment for himself, and the sheep have no wool. Having heard this, the sheep fled into the plain.
versions.evidence_quote: Frederik Kortlandt, Leiden University, www.kortlandt.nl SCHLEICHER’S FABLE [...] As my chief concern has always been the relative chronology of linguistic developments, it may be appropriate to present my version of Schleicher’s fable for a number of successive reconstructed systems,
versions.notation_notes: Since the distinction between the three laryngeals was preserved in Greek (Central IE) and Armenian (satəm IE), it was not lost before Balto-Slavic times, when they merged with the glottalic feature of the PIE “unaspirated voiced” stops into a glottal stop (Winter’s law, cf. K263 = 2009: 44f.). [...] The word-final fortis stop became glottalic in the non-Anatolian languages (cf. K272 = 2010: 40).
versions.notes: Stage column headed 'SATƏM INDO-EUROPEAN' in the paper, which gives the fable for successive reconstructed systems (PIE, non-Anatolian IE, Classic IE, Central IE, satəm IE, Balto-Slavic, East Baltic, Lithuanian); the Balto-Slavic, East Baltic and Lithuanian columns are not PIE-lineage and were omitted. English is Kortlandt's 'Translation of the text (cf. Lehmann & Zgusta 1979: 456, 462)', given once for all stages; per-line English assigned by its four sentences. Lines split at sentence-final periods (4 sentences); table line breaks joined with single spaces. Paper has no notation section; notation_notes are verbatim commentary sentences from p.1. See also 'An outline of Proto-Indo-European' (art269e.pdf, same publications list, not fetched). Text taken from the self-archived web PDF (271e); not collated against the printed 2010 pages. Source sets the labialization w as a superscript (text layer: plain 'w' with superscript flag); rendered here as U+02B7 ʷ. All other characters copied byte-for-byte from the PDF text layer (k/g + U+0311 combining inverted breve for palatovelars, U+2019 ’ for glottalic marks, ':' fortis marks, U+0294 ʔ, U+0295 ʕ) and checked against 300-dpi page renders; no Unicode normalization applied.
